text: **Official papers are linked, never copied.** Pearson owns its question papers, source material, mark schemes and examiners' reports. Every official item below opens on qualifications.pearson.com. This site hosts no copy of any of them and links to no paper-sharing site.

**RCF papers are labelled on every page that carries them.** They are written by RCF English in the format of the examination. They are not past papers, not sample assessment materials, and not endorsed by Pearson Edexcel.
**RCF English is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by Pearson Edexcel.** Pearson owns its assessment materials and its name and logo, neither of which appears on any RCF material.

blocks.title: Why Paper 2 first for Edexcel
text: Paper 2 carries 96 of the 160 marks and 60% of the qualification, and it is the paper with the question type students find hardest - the two-part Question 7. It is the more useful practice paper of the two.
An Edexcel Paper 1 model paper needs an original 19th-century fiction extract and will follow.

There is also an [AQA Paper 2 model paper](global-english/gcse/aqa/papers/rcf-model-paper-2/), which pairs a 19th-century source with a modern one. That pairing belongs to AQA's format, not Edexcel's - Edexcel puts its 19th-century text on Paper 1.

items.q: Where can I get Edexcel English Language past papers free?
a: From Pearson's own qualification page for 1EN0, which publishes past question papers, mark schemes and examiners' reports free of charge under its course materials and exam materials sections. It is linked at the top of this page.

items.q: Is the RCF model paper a real Edexcel paper?
a: No, and it says so on every page that carries it. It follows Edexcel's published structure - the same duration, sections, question types and marks - using two source texts and nine questions written by RCF English that have never appeared in an examination.

items.q: Can I use AQA past papers to revise for Edexcel?
a: Only for the underlying skills. The papers differ in length, marks, weighting and question structure: AQA Paper 2 pairs a 19th-century source with a modern one, while Edexcel Paper 2 uses two texts from the 20th and 21st centuries and adds a separate synthesis question. Practise the skills anywhere; practise the format on your own board's papers.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: This is **not** a Pearson Edexcel examination paper, past paper or sample assessment material. It is original practice material written by RCF English.

It follows the published structure of **Pearson Edexcel GCSE English Language 1EN0, Paper 2: Non-fiction and Transactional Writing**: 2 hours 5 minutes, 96 marks, two unseen non-fiction extracts from the 20th and 21st centuries linked by a theme, seven reading questions worth 56 marks, and a choice of transactional writing task worth 40 marks.
**RCF English is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by Pearson Edexcel.** For official papers see the [papers page](global-english/gcse/edexcel/papers/).

blocks.heading: Paper details
rows: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) English Language, specification 1EN0
Section A Reading, 56 marks, all questions. Section B Writing, 40 marks, one question.
Spend about 1 hour 20 minutes on Section A and about 45 minutes on Section B.

blocks.title: Before you start
text: Work to time. Answer **all** questions in Section A and **one** in Section B.
The marking guide is on a [separate page](global-english/gcse/edexcel/papers/rcf-model-paper-2-mark-scheme/). Do not open it until you have finished.
To print this paper, use your browser's print command and choose Save as PDF if you want a file.

blocks.heading: Text 1
text: **An original RCF passage.** From a memoir published in 1961, in which the writer recalls leaving a Yorkshire village at seventeen to work in a Leeds bakery.

parts.heading: From Nothing but the Ovens (original RCF text, 20th century)
text: **1** My mother packed for me, because I had never packed for anything, and she put in three of everything and a jar of her damson jam that broke somewhere between Skipton and Leeds and made a purple map of the whole case. I remember standing on the platform holding it and understanding, in a way I had not understood at home, that nobody here knew who my father was.

**5** The bakery was on a street I could not pronounce for a fortnight. Mr Cowan took me on because his brother had known my uncle, which is how everything worked then, and he said two things to me on the first morning. The first was that I would start at four. The second was that if I was late he would not shout at me, he would simply give the job to somebody else, and he said it so pleasantly that I was never once late in three years.

**11** Four o'clock in a bakery is not the middle of the night. It is a different country. The ovens had been banked since eleven and the whole building held its heat like a stone left in the sun, and you came in out of a black wet street into that, and for about ten seconds it was the finest thing in the world. Then you started work and it was merely hot.

**16** I was homesick in a way I would not have admitted to anyone, least of all myself. It came at odd hours - never at four in the morning, when there was too much to do, but at about half past nine when the first delivery had gone and there was a pause. I would stand in the yard with a mug of tea and think about the lane at home, and then Mr Cowan would put his head out and say something about the second batch and I would be perfectly all right again.

**23** What I could not have told anyone at seventeen, and can say easily enough now, is that the work saved me. Not the money, though the money mattered. It was that at four in the morning nobody has any interest in whether you are lonely. The dough does not care. It rises at its own rate and it must be dealt with at a particular moment and not five minutes later, and there is a great deal of comfort in being needed by something so entirely indifferent to you.

**30** I went home at Christmas with a coat I had bought myself and my mother cried, which I had not expected, and my father shook my hand, which I had expected even less. Neither of them asked whether I was happy. I think they knew that at seventeen it was not the question, and that I would have got it wrong if they had asked.

blocks.heading: Text 2
text: **An original RCF passage.** From an online column published in 2021, in which the writer describes six months working alone at a remote weather station.

parts.heading: From The Only One Here (original RCF text, 21st century, literary non-fiction)
text: **1** People ask what I did about the loneliness, and the honest answer is that I made a spreadsheet. This is not the reply anyone wants. They are hoping for something about the vastness of the sky. But six months alone on a headland with a rain gauge does not turn you into a poet; it turns you into a person with systems.

**6** The systems were about the day having edges. At home the day has edges built into it by other people - somebody arrives, somebody leaves, somebody wants something at half past three. Alone, the day is a long grey corridor and you have to put the doors in yourself. So: readings at six, ten, two, six and ten. Bread on Tuesdays. The long walk on Sundays whatever the weather, which in February was a decision I came to resent bitterly and never once broke.

**14** I had assumed the hard part would be the silence. It was not. The hard part was that nothing I did mattered to anyone in the moment I did it. The readings went into a database and were presumably useful to somebody eventually, but nobody was ever waiting for them. For the first six weeks I found this unbearable in a way I could not name, and then one evening I understood: I had never in my life done work that nobody was waiting for.

**21** What changed was not the loneliness but my opinion of it. Somewhere around week nine I stopped experiencing solitude as an absence of people and started experiencing it as a presence of time. That sounds like the sky-and-poetry answer I said I would not give, and I apologise, but there is no plainer way to put it. I had eleven hours a day that belonged to nobody. It took me two months to stop wasting them and one more to start looking forward to them.

**29** I would not do it again. I want to be clear about that, because these accounts always end in conversion and mine does not. I missed my sister's birthday and a friend's bad year and I cannot get those back, and the person who came off that headland was not wiser, only better at being by himself, which is a smaller and stranger prize than it sounds.

**35** But I keep the spreadsheet. It is on my laptop still, six months of readings in five columns, and every so often I open it for no reason at all. Nobody was waiting for those numbers. I put them in anyway. Some evenings that seems to me the most reliable thing I know about myself.

blocks.heading: Section A: Reading
text: Answer **all** questions in this section. You should spend about 1 hour 20 minutes on the whole of Section A. **[56 marks]**
**Read Text 1. Then answer Questions 1 to 3.**

parts.heading: Question 1
text: From lines 1 to 4, identify **two** things that happened on the writer's journey to Leeds. **(Total for Question 1 = 2 marks)**

parts.heading: Question 2
text: From lines 5 to 10, give **two** things Mr Cowan said to the writer on the first morning.
You may use your own words or quotations from the text. **(Total for Question 2 = 2 marks)**

parts.heading: Question 3
text: Analyse how the writer uses language and structure to interest and engage the reader. **(Total for Question 3 = 15 marks)**
In your answer you should write about:
bullets: language features and techniques
structure and organisation
supporting your views with detailed reference to the text

parts.heading: Text 2
text: **Read Text 2. Then answer Questions 4 to 6.**

parts.heading: Question 4
text: From lines 6 to 13, identify **one** thing the writer did on the same day each week. **(Total for Question 4 = 1 mark)**

parts.heading: Question 5
text: From lines 14 to 20, identify **one** thing the writer had assumed before going to the headland. **(Total for Question 5 = 1 mark)**

parts.heading: Question 6
text: In this extract, the writer attempts to show that solitude changed him in a way he did not expect.
Evaluate how successfully this is achieved.
Support your views with detailed reference to the text. **(Total for Question 6 = 15 marks)**

parts.heading: Question 7
text: **Question 7 is about Text 1 and Text 2. Answer both parts of the question.**

parts.heading: Question 7 (a)
text: The two texts show people working away from home.
What similarities do these experiences share in these extracts?
Use evidence from **both** texts to support your answer. **(6 marks)**

parts.heading: Question 7 (b)
text: Compare how the writers of Text 1 and Text 2 present ideas and perspectives about what work gave them. Support your answer with detailed references to both texts. **(14 marks)**
You should write about:
bullets: the ideas and perspectives
how they are presented
how they are similar or different

parts.heading: End of Section A
text: **(Total for Question 7 = 20 marks)**
**TOTAL FOR SECTION A = 56 MARKS**

blocks.heading: Section B: Transactional Writing
text: Answer **ONE** question in this section. You should spend about 45 minutes on this section.
Indicate which question you are answering. **[40 marks]**

parts.heading: Question 8
text: *"Young people should be encouraged to leave home for work or study, even when there is no need to."*
Write an article for a magazine read by parents in which you explain your point of view on this statement. **(Total for Question 8 = 40 marks)**

parts.heading: Question 9
text: Your local college has asked former students to write to next year's intake about living away from home for the first time.
Write a letter to those students giving your advice. **(Total for Question 9 = 40 marks)**
**TOTAL FOR SECTION B = 40 MARKS**
**TOTAL FOR PAPER = 96 MARKS**

It is **not** a Pearson Edexcel mark scheme. The band descriptions below are RCF English's own plain-English account of how marks divide; no Edexcel mark scheme wording is reproduced. blocks.heading: The short questions
blocks.caption: Six marks in total. One mark per acceptable point; do not credit more than the number asked for.
rows: Any two: her mother packed for her; three of everything was packed; a jar of damson jam was included; the jam jar broke; the jam stained the whole case; she stood on the platform holding it
That she would start at four o'clock; that if she was late he would not shout but would give the job to somebody else
Baked bread (on Tuesdays), or took the long walk (on Sundays). Either is acceptable; only one is required.
That the hard part would be the silence

blocks.heading: Question 3: language and structure in Text 1 (15 marks)
text: AO2. Reward analysis of effect, supported by short quotations. Both language **and** structure must be covered for the higher bands.

parts.heading: Indicative content: language
bullets: **"made a purple map of the whole case"** - a domestic accident turned into an image of territory, which quietly introduces the idea of a journey into unknown country.
**"nobody here knew who my father was"** - stated flatly, with no comment, so the reader supplies the mixture of fear and freedom the writer does not name.

**"Four o'clock in a bakery is not the middle of the night. It is a different country."** - a short denial followed by a shorter assertion; the metaphor of a country returns and links back to the map of jam.
**"held its heat like a stone left in the sun"** - a simile that makes warmth feel stored and patient rather than active.
**"The dough does not care."** - four blunt words placed after a long sentence, giving the paragraph's central idea the force of a conclusion.
**"so entirely indifferent to you"** - the writer chooses comfort in indifference, which reverses what a reader expects loneliness to need.

parts.heading: Indicative content: structure
bullets: Opens with the mother packing, not with the arrival, so the reader leaves home with the writer.
Moves in clear stages: journey, employer, the ovens, homesickness, understanding, and the return home at Christmas.
The homesickness paragraph is placed after the description of the heat, so warmth and loneliness sit side by side.
Time shifts in the fifth paragraph - "could not have told anyone at seventeen, and can say easily enough now" - separating the girl who lived it from the woman writing.
Ends on the parents' silence rather than on the writer's feelings, which leaves the reader to judge.

parts.heading: Bands, in plain English
bullets: **13-15** Perceptive analysis of how language and structure work together; judicious short quotations; terminology accurate and used only where it helps.
**10-12** Detailed analysis; both language and structure covered; effects explained.
**7-9** Clear explanation of effects; some analysis; both areas touched, one more thinly.
**4-6** Some comment on effect; features identified; structure may be neglected.
**1-3** Simple identification; effect asserted rather than explained.
**0** Nothing to reward.

blocks.heading: Question 6: evaluation of Text 2 (15 marks)
text: AO4. Reward judgement supported by reference. A candidate who only analyses method, without saying how successfully the writer achieves the stated purpose, cannot reach the higher bands.

parts.heading: Indicative content: agreeing that it is successful
bullets: The writer names the expected answer and refuses it - "They are hoping for something about the vastness of the sky" - which makes the change he does report more believable.
The change is defined precisely: solitude experienced not as "an absence of people" but as "a presence of time".
It is dated and staged - week nine, two months, one more - so the reader watches it happen rather than being told about it.
The refusal of a happy ending, "I would not do it again", protects the account from sounding like an advertisement.
The spreadsheet returns at the end, and its meaning has changed since paragraph one, which shows the change rather than asserting it.

parts.heading: Indicative content: qualifying
bullets: The writer admits the phrasing sounds like the answer he mocked - "that sounds like the sky-and-poetry answer" - so a reader may feel the insight is thinner than the build-up promised.
The costs are listed but not examined: the missed birthday and the friend's bad year get one sentence between them.
"Better at being by himself" is deliberately small, and a reader may judge that the piece proves a minor change rather than an unexpected one.

parts.heading: Bands, in plain English
bullets: **13-15** Perceptive evaluation; a clear judgement sustained and supported by well-chosen references.
**10-12** Detailed evaluation; judgements made and supported.
**7-9** Clear evaluative comment; a position taken with some support.
**4-6** Some judgement, largely descriptive.
**1-3** Analysis or summary with no evaluation.
**0** Nothing to reward.

blocks.heading: Question 7(a): synthesis (6 marks)
text: AO1. Similarities of content, with evidence from both texts. Do not reward analysis of method here - that belongs to 7(b).
bullets: **Both found the work harder emotionally than practically.** Text 1: homesickness "came at odd hours". Text 2: "the hard part was that nothing I did mattered to anyone".

**Both were changed by being needed, or not needed, by the work itself.** Text 1: comfort in being needed by something "so entirely indifferent". Text 2: "I had never in my life done work that nobody was waiting for".
**Both imposed or accepted a strict routine.** Text 1: starting at four, never once late in three years. Text 2: readings at six, ten, two, six and ten; the Sunday walk "never once broke".
**Both withhold the emotional conclusion a reader expects.** Text 1 ends on the parents not asking whether she was happy. Text 2 states plainly "I would not do it again".
Three developed similarities, each with evidence from both texts, is a full answer.

items.label: Original RCF model answer
items.prompt: Compare how the writers of Text 1 and Text 2 present ideas and perspectives about what work gave them.
sample: Both writers believe their work gave them something they had not gone looking for, but they present that discovery very differently. The writer of Text 1 arrives at it late and states it plainly: "the work saved me". The verb is enormous and it is used without any softening, and because the paragraph before it has been about standing in a yard with a mug of tea, the plainness lands as honesty rather than exaggeration. The writer of Text 2 refuses that kind of statement entirely. He offers the reader a deflating joke instead - "the honest answer is that I made a spreadsheet" - and only allows his real claim to appear once he has apologised for it in advance. Where Text 1 trusts a large word to carry a large meaning, Text 2 distrusts every large word it uses, and both methods work, because each suits the person speaking.

The two also differ in how they explain what the work did. Text 1 locates the value outside the writer, in the dough that "rises at its own rate" and "does not care", and the short blunt sentences give that indifference a kind of solidity. The comfort is in being subordinate to something real. Text 2 locates the value inside the writer, in "a presence of time" that belonged to nobody, and the abstract phrasing shows a man who has thought about his experience for a long time rather than one who lived it and moved on. Text 1 presents work as a structure imposed on a lonely girl; Text 2 presents solitude as a space a man eventually learned to occupy.

Finally, both writers withhold the ending the reader expects, but they withhold different things. Text 1 closes on the parents, not on the writer: "neither of them asked whether I was happy", and the emotion is left entirely in the reader's hands. Text 2 closes on the writer alone with the spreadsheet, and states the refusal directly - "I would not do it again" - before offering the quiet final image. Text 1 is the more moving because it says less; Text 2 is the more convincing because it has already admitted what the experience cost.
notes: **Both writers appear in every paragraph.** No paragraph could be split in half without collapsing, which is the single most important requirement of this question.
**Ideas and presentation are handled together.** Each paragraph names the difference in perspective, then analyses the writing that conveys it - the assessment objective asks for both.
**Comparative connectives do real work:** *Where Text 1 trusts... Text 2 distrusts*; *Text 1 locates... Text 2 locates*.
**Each paragraph ends by weighing.** The final sentence of each judges the two against each other rather than summarising them.
**Quotations are short and embedded**, which leaves room for analysis in about eighteen minutes.
**Length.** Three developed paragraphs. A fourth thin paragraph would score lower than these three.

blocks.heading: Section B: transactional writing (40 marks)
text: Mark communication and organisation separately from vocabulary, sentence structure, spelling and punctuation. Mark content first - it is the mark most often given too generously.

parts.heading: Communication and organisation
bullets: **Top band.** Form, purpose and audience are unmistakable from the opening lines and sustained throughout. A single line of argument, deliberately structured, with paragraph lengths varied for effect.
**Middle band.** Form is recognisable and the argument is clear, but the structure is even and the audience is addressed only generally.
**Lower band.** The form is uncertain or abandoned; points are listed rather than developed.
A concession answered - *it is true that..., but* - is the most reliable single lift from middle to top.

parts.heading: Vocabulary, sentence structures, spelling and punctuation
bullets: **Top band.** A wide range of sentence forms used for effect; ambitious vocabulary used accurately; demanding punctuation correct.
**Middle band.** Some variety; mostly accurate; errors do not obscure meaning.
**Lower band.** Limited range; errors slow the reader.
An error-free piece with no range belongs in the middle band, not the top.

items.label: Original RCF model answer - a letter of advice (about 480 words)
items.prompt: Your local college has asked former students to write to next year's intake about living away from home for the first time. Write a letter to those students giving your advice.
sample: I have been asked to tell you what living away from home is like, and I want to start by warning you that most of the advice you are about to receive this summer is wrong. You will be told it is the best year of your life. It was not the best year of mine. It was, however, the year I became somebody I could rely on, and that turned out to be worth more.

The first thing nobody mentions is that homesickness does not arrive when you expect it. It will not come on the first night, when you are too busy and too frightened. It arrives about three weeks in, on an ordinary Tuesday, for no reason at all. When it does, please understand that there is nothing wrong with you and nothing wrong with your decision. Everyone on your corridor is having the same Tuesday. Almost none of them will say so.

My second piece of advice is duller and more useful: give your week some edges. At home the shape of your day is made by other people - somebody calls you down for a meal, somebody wants the bathroom, somebody expects you back. Alone, all of that disappears at once, and a week with no fixed points in it is a surprisingly bleak thing. So fix some. One class you never miss. One evening you always cook properly. One walk you take on Sundays whatever the weather. They sound trivial. They are what stops the term becoming a long grey corridor.

Third: be careful about the friendships of the first fortnight. You will meet people in a state of mild panic and mistake relief for affection. Some of those friendships will last thirty years; most will not survive until Christmas, and that is not a failure. Keep the door open, keep meeting people in October and November as well as September, and do not decide who you are in your first week and then spend two years defending it.

It is true that some of you will find this easier than I am making it sound. A few of you will step off the train entirely at home in yourselves, and I was envious of those people at the time. What I did not know then is that they had simply arrived at the difficult part earlier or would arrive at it later. Nobody skips it.
One last thing. Ring home more often than you feel like ringing home, and less often than they would like you to. Somewhere in that gap is a person who is managing.
You will manage. Most of what you need you already have, and the rest of it you will build out of ordinary Tuesdays.
notes: **Form is unmistakable.** A salutation, sustained direct address to a named audience, and a formal sign-off. An examiner identifies the form from the first line.
**Audience is specific throughout** - not "young people" but the students who will step off that train, addressed as *you*.

**Communication and organisation, top band.** One line of argument held from opening to close: this will be harder than you are being told, and that is survivable. Three numbered pieces of advice, then a concession, then a short closing turn.
**The concession does real work.** *It is true that some of you will find this easier* is answered rather than dismissed, which is what lifts a piece out of the middle band.
**Range and accuracy.** Sentence lengths vary sharply; the shortest sentence, *Nobody skips it*, is placed at the argument's turn. The semicolon, the dash and the colon are all used correctly.
**Concrete detail instead of invented statistics** - the ordinary Tuesday, the corridor, the Sunday walk - which persuades further than a percentage would.
**The ending returns to the opening image**, so the letter finishes rather than stopping.
